# Insights and Recommendations

*Generated by `src/insights.py`; every number is computed from the data and model outputs. Findings are associations in observational data, not causal effects.*

## Key findings

| # | theme | finding | key number | source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| F1 | Market concentration | 90.6% of the 9,551 restaurants are in India and 83.2% are in Delhi NCR alone. | 83.2% | data/processed/zomato_clean.csv |
| F2 | Price range and popularity | The share of High-popularity restaurants rises from 13.3% in price range 1 to 63.2% in range 3 (55.0% in range 4); average rating rises from 3.24 to 3.89. | 13.3% -> 63.2% | rated restaurants; EDA chi-square and Kruskal-Wallis tests |
| F3 | Table booking (India) | In India (rated restaurants), 63.0% of restaurants with table booking are High-popularity, against 27.6% without; mean rating 3.55 vs 3.31. | 63.0% vs 27.6% | rated Indian restaurants; EDA Mann-Whitney and chi-square tests |
| F4 | Online delivery (India) | In India (rated restaurants), delivery outlets are more often High-popularity (44.6% vs 27.2%), but their mean rating is almost the same (3.37 vs 3.34): delivery goes with more votes, not better ratings. Delivery exists only in India and the UAE. | 44.6% vs 27.2% | rated Indian restaurants; EDA Mann-Whitney test |
| F5 | Votes and rating | Votes and rating are strongly linked (Spearman rho = 0.68). The target is built from votes, so votes, rating and anything derived from them are excluded from the model's features. | rho 0.68 | outputs/eda_statistics.csv |
| F6 | Unrated restaurants | 2,148 restaurants (22.5%) have no rating yet; only 4.5% of them offer online delivery, against 31.8% of rated ones. | 2,148 (22.5%) | docs/unrated_restaurants.md |
| F7 | Popularity model | The honest model (Gradient Boosting) reaches 61.3% accuracy against a 33.6% baseline. Location is its strongest signal: without location features accuracy falls to 51.9%. | 61.3% | docs/model_results.md |
| F8 | Medium class | Accuracy is 44.8% for restaurants within 5 percentile points of a class cut-off and 79.3% for those far from it. Telling High from Low alone (a separate, easier question) reaches 83.2%. | 44.8% vs 79.3% | docs/model_results.md |

## Recommendations

| # | recommendation | based on | why |
|---|---|---|---|
| R1 | Choose the location first | F1, F7 | Location and locality carry the most signal for popularity; compare candidate localities before deciding cuisine or price. Caveat: outside Delhi NCR the data lists mostly well-known restaurants, so part of the location effect reflects how Zomato sampled cities. |
| R2 | Offer table booking where the format allows it | F3 | It goes with a much higher share of High-popularity restaurants (association, not proof of cause). |
| R3 | Use delivery for reach, not for rating | F4 | In India, delivery goes with a higher High-popularity share (44.6% vs 27.2%) but ratings barely differ (3.37 vs 3.34); service quality still drives the rating. |
| R4 | Mind the price band | F2 | Mid and upper price ranges are more often High-popularity; budget outlets compete in a crowded, lower-voted segment. |
| R5 | Help unrated restaurants get their first ratings | F6 | A fifth of listings have no rating; platform prompts or owner follow-up would make them comparable. |
| R6 | Use the model as a screen, not a verdict | F7, F8 | It separates likely High from likely Low well; Medium predictions near a cut-off are uncertain. |
